paragraphs: This one too is one of the ignorant dissenters; namely, that he permitted [marriage and intercourse, the] "lawful pleasures of worldly things." It was [my view], and the view of others, that he it was who innovated this doctrine; but one of the elders of the ʿUkbarīs informed me that he took it from some of the people of the mountains, and that it is no unbelief, for innovations are many among the people of the mountains — only that Mīshawayh brought it forth, publicized it, and argued for it.

Mīshawayh claimed that the Festival of Weeks must be on a Sunday, but he does not know which Sunday. This doctrine belongs also to a group of the Baṣrans, except that [their] reckoning was with the majority. He claimed that the Passover must always be on a Thursday, so that the Day of Atonement be on the Sabbath; for it is said of it [Lev 23:32]: "שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן." The meaning, with him: two Sabbaths — one the Sabbath, the other the Day of Atonement. He was in doubt about the knowledge of the heads of the months — not knowing by what [criterion] they must be taken.
They reported that he used to say to his adherents: "All the [received] tradition (qabbalah) is easy. Hold to what is in your hands" — meaning the festival of the majority.

He claimed that on the Sabbath no offering may be brought at all, and that the saying of Scripture [Num 28:10] "עֹלַת שַׁבַּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ" means "for the Sabbath," and that it used to be offered before the Sabbath for the sake of the Sabbath.
He claimed that the prayer-direction (qibla), in every place, must be toward the west, and that whoever is in Egypt or the West turns toward the Temple when he prays.

: Arabic al-lawāʾib min al-ṣawāʾib al-dunyawiyya — a distinctive doctrine of Mīshawayh permitting marriage and sexual relations. See Erder, The Karaite Mourners of Zion, ch. 3 (pp. 167–307), the most extensive treatment of Mīshawayh al-ʿUkbarī in the scholarship.
: Mīshawayh's calendar — two Sabbaths (an ordinary Sabbath + the Day of Atonement) = "shabbat shabbaton," requiring Passover always on a Thursday.
: Arabic qibla, the direction of prayer; Mīshawayh held it is always westward, even when one is not facing the Temple — the height of geographical extremism.
